title: GPU Evacuation Heuristics and Bridge Node Patterns (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working draft of heuristics and small runbook fragments used during GPU and node-level failures. The goal is to capture pragmatic, low-friction actions an oncall can take in the first 5-30 minutes to stabilize customer traffic and buy time for hardware replacement or capacity injection.

Scope and assumptions:
- Targets: single-node GPU faults, thermal trips, degraded PCIe fabric, and small cluster-wide capacity deficits (up to ~10% of serving pool).
- Assumes access to cluster control plane (kubectl, internal admin APIs) and oncall permissions for the capacity orchestrator and inventory system.
- Not a complete teardown — this complements the full hardware replacement SOP maintained by datacenter/ops.

Quick heuristics (first 5 minutes):
1) Verify the alert/context: check alert source (prometheus / router / runtime). Is it a single GPU OOM, a node unreachable, or higher-level SLO breach?
2) Check recent deploys: glance at recent model rollouts and traffic spike graphs (console -> routes). If a rollout happened within 15 minutes, consider rollback as a fast mitigation.
3) Immediate soft-mitigation: if memory/thermal issues on a node, toggle routing weight to 0 for that node's zone (routing policy), or mark node as low-priority in pool. Prefer traffic steering over global throttles.

Cordon & drain pattern (safe-short):
- When to cordon: node shows repeated GPU errors, unstable NVLink fabric, or kernel driver resets.
- Command examples (internal):
  - kubectl cordon <node-name>
  - kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=60
- Notes: use --grace-period short for emergency evacuations but monitor in-flight requests; streaming sessions can be disrupted. Prefer route-level fallback for live chat endpoints.

Bridge nodes and temporary capacity tips:
- The “bridge node” concept: a pre-baked node image with minimal runtime + lighter model variants to accept overflow traffic during GPU replacement.
- Prep steps (pre-incident): maintain a hotpool of 2–4 bridge nodes in each zone for fastest oncall spin-up. These nodes run quantized/half-precision variants and a slim runtime to reduce memory pressure.
- On incident: switch a percentage of traffic to bridge nodes via smart-routing rule (console -> routing -> policy). Start 1 bridge node per every 50 connections routed away from the degraded pool.

GPU hot-swap checklist (ops handoff friendly):
- Before physical swap (oncall): annotate node with incident id and note critical services running. Ensure capacity shim in place (bridge nodes or cross-zone spillover).
- During swap (ops): confirm GPU carrier seated, power-cycling sequence complete, driver reflash if required.
- After swap (oncall/ops): run smoke tests: small synthetic prompts to the model endpoints, verify KV cache warmup, confirm no OOMs for 5m at baseline traffic.

KV/prefix cache and model cache notes:
- Draining a node may evict cached prefixes; to avoid a stampede on backend, stagger drain operations and keep a small client-side backoff.
- If prefix cache miss rate spikes > 5% for >3 min, partially route traffic to cached model variants.

Cluster warmup and capacity onramp (fastpath):
1) Add nodes to autoscaler group or allocate reserved capacity pool.
2) Immediately mark new nodes as warm candidates; do not fully open to 100% until KV cache priming completes. Use route weights 10% -> 30% -> 60% over 15 min windows.
3) Monitor tail latency (p99/p995), token generation CPU/GPU utilization, and request queue length. If tail latency increases more than 30% from baseline, throttle roll-in.

Decision matrix (short):
- Node flapping with repeated reboots: cordon + isolate; escalate to hardware team.
- Single GPU error but node stable: move running pods off GPU slot if possible; use model fallback to CPU-only variant until swap.
- Zone-level degradation: enable cross-zone spillover, notify platform leads, and consider evacuating non-critical workloads.

SCRIPTS & COMMANDS (notes-to-self):
- internal get node status: rcli node status --name <node>
- quick cordon/drain helper: scripts/evacuate-node --node <node> --mode emergency
- route weight change: rcli routing set-weight --route prod/chat --node-pool degraded_pool --weight 0.2

Metrics to watch in the first 30 minutes:
- routing errors/sec, failed requests, p50/p95/p99 latency per route, GPU memory pressure, kernel-driver-reset count, pod evictions, queue depth.
- Business signal: number of active sessions, number of timed-out user responses (chat).

Oncall communication template (use in Slack incident channel):
- Subject: [INCIDENT] node gpu-12 thermal trip -> cordoned 
- TL;DR: cordoned node gpu-12 in us-west2; routing weight reduced 80% to bridge nodes; working with ops for hot-swap.
- Actions taken: cordon/drain, spun up 2 bridge nodes, primed cache, smoke tests passing.
- Next steps: ops swap ETA 45m, monitor p99 and KV miss rate.

Post-incident checklist:
- Confirm hardware replacement ticket closed and serial numbers updated in inventory.
- Rebalance model placement to reclaim bridge capacity.
- Run incident retro: capture timeline, decision points, what worked, what didn't.
- Update this doc with any temporary commands or corner cases found.

Gaps / open questions (draft):
- We need a non-disruptive streaming session handoff pattern so drains don't sever long-running chats.
- Consider an automated small-signal traffic probe to validate warmup before routing more than 10% to new nodes.
- Need a standardized incident annotation mechanism across control-plane systems.

References and helpful reads (internal):
- internal runbook index: https://confluence.redwood/internal/sre/runbooks
- HW swap SOP: ops-playbooks/physical-gpu-replace-v2
- Slack channel: #sre-oncall, #infra-hardware

Notes-to-self: this doc should remain short and pragmatic. Avoid re-copying the full ops SOP; focus on what the first responder can do to keep customers online and provide a clean handoff to ops for repair.
